title: gc: decide value-aware live eviction from tombstone and shadow data

labels.name: area:local
labels.description: Local cache engine: cache-key, store, hardlink/reflink restore, RUSTC_WRAPPER hot path (no daemon)

body:
Status (2026-09-11): step 1 landed in https://github.com/kunobi-ninja/kache/pull/598, step 2 in https://github.com/kunobi-ninja/kache/pull/604, and the step 4 shadow policy in https://github.com/kunobi-ninja/kache/pull/676. Live eviction is still size-driven. What remains is estimating reuse from the tombstones and deciding whether a two-sided observation ledger replaces the latest-eviction tombstones.

## Problem

Eviction scores entries by size, with no notion of what an entry costs to rebuild:

```rust
// originally src/store.rs, Store::evict(); eviction now lives in crates/kache-store
score = (hit_count + 1) / (hours_since_last_access * size_mb)   // evict lowest first
```

kache already records `compile_time_ms` on every entry — the exact cost of a miss on that key — but it lives only in the entry's `meta.json` and is **not a column in the `entries` table**, so the eviction query cannot see it. The cache therefore cannot distinguish an artifact that took 6 seconds to build from one that took 0.3 seconds.

## Evidence that size is a poor proxy for rebuild cost

Measured on a real 46.5 GB / 51,562-entry store (1,500-entry sample with both size and compile time):

- log-log correlation(size, compile_time) = **0.73**
- value density spans **~48x**: `png` 2.5 MB / 5.9 s rebuild (2.4 s per MB) versus `unicode_general_category` 5.8 MB / 0.3 s rebuild (0.05 s per MB)

Concretely, the current formula's first eviction victims in that store are `surrealdb_core` entries (≈590 MB, last used 15 hours ago) while it protects `lazy_static` (14 KB, rebuilds in tens of milliseconds). Size-based ordering is doing something reasonable for *disk reclamation per eviction*, but it is blind to the value being destroyed.

Related: 44.6% of stored bytes (20.75 GB) sit in entries that have never been reused, and 54% of `lib` entries have `hit_count = 0`.

## What I could NOT establish (and a correction)

I first simulated replacement policies by measuring "cached compile-time destroyed per GB freed" and found pure value-density (`compile_time / size`) beat the current policy 2.8x (84 vs 239 s lost per GB). **That result is not trustworthy and should not be used to justify a policy change.**

The simulation scores a policy by compile-time destroyed *at eviction time*, treating every cached entry as equally likely to be requested again. Pure `compile_time/size` optimizes exactly that quantity, so it wins by construction — the metric and the candidate policy are the same function. Cross-checked against two independent reviews, both of which identified this immediately.

What the simulation does legitimately show: the `1/idle_hours` term in the current formula is a poor model of reuse probability (every variant containing it scored worse than variants without it). That is an argument against *this particular* recency term, not against using recency information.

## The correct objective

Minimize expected future recompilation cost subject to the byte cap. For an eviction decision:

```
retention_value_per_byte =
    P(key requested again before it becomes obsolete / within horizon T)
      × net_rebuild_cost
      / size
```

Evict lowest. The important structural point: **reuse probability multiplies rebuild cost** — it is not an independent denominator or an arbitrary recency divisor. Recency, age, and hit count are *features for estimating that probability*, not terms to be bolted onto the score directly.

`net_rebuild_cost` should be compile time minus the cost of serving from cache.

Note this cache has a distinctive property: keys go **permanently dead** when a dependency version or compiler flag changes. That exact key will never be requested again, at any age. So the relevant quantity is closer to "probability the key is still live" than to classic web-cache recency.

## Why the reuse data in hand cannot answer this

Reuse-by-age from the same store:

| age | entries | % ever reused |
|---|---|---|
| <1d | 1535 | 2% |
| 1-3d | 7119 | 28% |
| 3-7d | 15642 | 63% |
| 7-30d | 13710 | 36% |
| >30d | 13556 | 52% |

Non-monotonic, and unusable as a probability estimate because of: right-censoring (young entries have had no time to be reused), survivorship/policy bias (what remains was selected by the current policy — evicted entries are invisible), unequal exposure, cohort confounding (age correlates with different projects and dependency eras), and the fact that "ever reused so far" is not "will be reused after eviction".

## Proposed work

1. **Index `compile_time_ms` on `entries`** (migration + backfill from `meta.json`). Cheap, unblocks everything below, and useful on its own for `kache stats` / `report` — "what is this cache actually worth in saved compile time" is currently unanswerable from the index.
2. **Tombstones + prospective telemetry.** On eviction, retain a small record (key, features at decision time, evicted_at). When a later lookup misses on a tombstoned key, log it. That is the only way to observe post-eviction demand, which is exactly what the snapshot cannot show. Bounded and cheap: a key row plus a timestamp.
3. **Estimate reuse from that stream**, conditioning on idle time, age, hit count, and key class, with censoring handled properly. Validate on a later time window.
4. **Shadow-evaluate policies** against recorded traces before changing production behavior; compare current, pure density, and probability-weighted scores on total future recompilation time, not on inventory value.
5. Only then change `Store::evict()`.

Step 1 is worth doing regardless of whether the policy ever changes. Step 2 is the measurement that makes the rest honest.

## Related

- #186 (reachability-based GC) — different axis, same subsystem
- #509 (`kache gc` reports "evicted 0 entries" while over the limit)
- #319 / `cache_executables` — if executables are ever cached by default they are large and expensive, making value-aware eviction materially more important than it is today
